blocks.text: 大约一年前，我们开始测试 Claude 设计基础电子电路的能力。我们与 Diode Computers 合作1，这家公司专门设计和制造电路板。我们用它来训练 Claude 完成一些简单任务，比如阅读芯片的数据手册，并弄清楚芯片需要哪些外围元件才能工作。当时我们试验的模型还不能可靠地完成电路板布局，在设计相互匹配的元件时也很吃力。而现在，Claude 已经能够从头到尾设计和制作电子硬件原型。

inlines.text: 大约一年前，我们开始测试 Claude 设计基础电子电路的能力。我们
与 Diode Computers 合作
，这家公司专门设计和制造电路板。我们用它来训练 Claude 完成一些简单任务，比如阅读芯片的数据手册，并弄清楚芯片需要哪些外围元件才能工作。当时我们试验的模型还不能可靠地完成电路板布局，在设计相互匹配的元件时也很吃力。而现在，Claude 已经能够从头到尾设计和制作电子硬件原型。

blocks.text: 设计一台电子设备需要经历许多复杂步骤，还要应对各种实际约束。你不仅要设计和仿真电路板，还要考虑电路板的物理布局和实际表现，对机械部件建模，编写固件，同时还要随时掌握哪些元器件容易采购、工厂具备怎样的生产能力。

inlines.text: 设计一台电子设备需要经历许多复杂步骤，还要应对各种实际约束。你不仅要设计和仿真电路板，还要考虑电路板的物理布局和实际表现，对机械部件建模，编写固件，同时还要随时掌握哪些元器件容易采购、工厂具备怎样的生产能力。

blocks.text: 为了解新版 Claude 模型在这方面进步了多少，我们再次与 Diode 合作，这次让 Claude Fable 5.2 设计三款电子设备：一台免提扬声器、一个语音助手中枢和一只掌上虚拟宠物。只需极少的提示词，Claude 就能运用几何推理完成每块电路板的布局，预判制造约束，并确保设计方案在约束范围内可行。它会自行修改设计，在计算机辅助设计（CAD）软件中为设计建模，最后指导人类工程师制作出原型——这些原型的电路无需任何修改就能正常工作。

inlines.text: 为了解新版 Claude 模型在这方面进步了多少，我们再次与 Diode 合作，这次让 Claude Fable 5.2 设计三款电子设备：一台免提扬声器、一个语音助手中枢和一只掌上虚拟宠物。只需极少的提示词，Claude 就能运用几何推理完成每块电路板的布局，预判制造约束，并确保设计方案在约束范围内可行。它会自行修改设计，在计算机辅助设计（CAD）软件中为设计建模，最后指导人类工程师制作出原型——这些原型的电路无需任何修改就能正常工作。

blocks.text: 每个设计都从一条简单的提示词开始，我们只说明要造什么设备、主要硬件要求是什么。以扬声器的提示词为例，我们要求的是“一个通过 USB-C 连接电脑的圆盘形设备，内置麦克风和扬声器，支持蓝牙并配有 PCB 天线”。随后 Claude 编写设备规格、绘制清晰的原理图、确定元器件在印刷电路板（PCB）上的位置、布线连接各元器件的铜走线、设计可 3D 打印的外壳、编写固件，并整理出物料清单。Diode 在 Claude 的指导下组装电路板并运行固件。最终做出来的扬声器原型经过数周使用仍然正常工作。

blocks.text: 用几何推理解决问题

inlines.text: 用几何推理解决问题

blocks.text: Fable 5.2 与我们在早期测试中使用的模型相比，最大的差别在于它解决复杂几何问题的能力，比如元器件在电路板上怎么摆放、元器件之间的铜走线怎么布。

inlines.text: Fable 5.2 与我们在早期测试中使用的模型相比，最大的差别在于它解决复杂几何问题的能力，比如元器件在电路板上怎么摆放、元器件之间的铜走线怎么布。

blocks.text: 此前的模型一直难以决定如何安排基本元件——比如把支撑部件放得离它们所服务的芯片太远，或者连接器方向装反。相比之下，Fable 5.2 生成的布局更紧凑、更实用。它会优先布设最重要的连接：传输高速信号或大电流的，以及对噪声敏感的。例如，在设计语音助手中枢时，Claude 先布设 USB 和以太网连接，这类连接通过成对的走线传输信号——走线是电路板上细长的铜条。它一次布设一对走线，让每对中的两条走线长度一致、间距正确。它还加入了调谐图形——细小的锯齿状走线，用来延长某条走线，使信号同时到达——并安排电源各部分的位置以提高效率。

blocks.text: 为了展示 Fable 5.2 在电路板布局上比早期模型强多少，我们让 Diode 跑了 PCB Gym——这是一个内部基准测试，根据模型在已移除布局的电路板设计上放置元件和重新布线的表现打分。Fable 5.2 在该基准上得分 69%，而 Fable 5 只有 25%（图 2）。它在 BenchCAD 2.1 上表现也更好，这是一个公开基准，测试模型能否根据工程图纸和渲染图像重建 3D 零件、装配体和电路板。Fable 5.2 得分 83.5%，几乎是其前代 Claude Fable 5.1 的两倍。

blocks.text: 修改设计

inlines.text: 修改设计

blocks.text: 早期模型在设计 PCB 布局时很少修改自己的作品，即使已经明显看出它们选的布局永远无法完成连接布设。过去一年里，Diode 用这些模型设计了许多电路板，完成度达到 95%，却仍然无法使用。

inlines.text: 早期模型在设计 PCB 布局时很少修改自己的作品，即使已经明显看出它们选的布局永远无法完成连接布设。过去一年里，Diode 用这些模型设计了许多电路板，完成度达到 95%，却仍然无法使用。

blocks.text: 当 Claude 发现自己的某个设计行不通时，它会主动改变思路，无需外部提示。例如，在设计扬声器电话的电路板（有四层铜）时，它把信号重新分配到两颗芯片的不同引脚上。这样一来，扬声器电话触摸控制下方的走线就能保持在同一层，彼此不交叉。后来，当电路板背面变得过于拥挤时，Claude 交换了可互换引脚上的信号，并重新布设了电路板的一整个角落，而不是用额外的层间跳线来打补丁。

blocks.text: 在为语音助手中枢的设计文件布设走线时，Claude 注意到铜连接“变得太乱，无法用肉眼追踪”，并推理道：“我应该把这些走线[铜连接]全部拆掉，重新开始。”它随后删除并重新布设铜连接数十次，直到找到可行的方案。

blocks.text: 使用软件和文档

inlines.text: 使用软件和文档

blocks.text: 当某个设备的设计决策取决于特定元件的细节时，Claude 常常查阅该元件的数据手册——制造商发布的技术文档。当被问及手持宠物在没有电池的情况下能否工作时，Claude 阅读了充电器的数据手册，回答说它可以靠 USB 供电运行，但预测充电指示灯会闪烁，因为充电器会不断给替代电池位置的小电容反复充电。2

blocks.text: 为了给语音助手集线器布线，Claude 从 Diode 提供的设计软件入手，该软件让它能运行 KiCad 内置的布线器（一种绘制走线的工具），KiCad 是一款广泛使用的电路板设计程序。KiCad 的布线器在 Claude 选定的两点之间一次只画一条走线。但这个集线器有从 100 针连接器引出的长走线，Claude 判断逐条布线需要太多逐步指导。

blocks.text: 于是 Claude 自己写了一个布线器：一种把电路板划分成网格并搜索网格、为每条走线找到畅通路径的算法。大约半小时内，Claude 就有了一个布线器，能在约一秒内布好每条长走线。当 Claude 发现一条音频时钟走线离以太网走线太近时，它调整了布线器，在敏感走线周围留出更多空间。

blocks.text: 跟踪约束条件和下游影响

inlines.text: 跟踪约束条件和下游影响

blocks.text: 设计中某一部分做出的决策会产生下游影响，Claude 会跟踪这些影响。在设计每个设备的外壳时，它编写代码来检查电路板的 3D 模型能否装入外壳而不发生任何元件碰撞。例如，它发现扬声器电话的电路板无法直接向下放入外壳，因为静音开关会撞到后壁。Claude 算出，如果在安装时把电路板倾斜约 25 度就能装进去。它在 3D 模型中测试了这一点，并把该步骤加入了装配说明。

inlines.text: 设计中某一部分做出的决策会产生下游影响，Claude 会跟踪这些影响。在设计每个设备的外壳时，它编写代码来检查电路板的 3D 模型能否装入外壳而不发生任何元件碰撞。例如，它发现扬声器电话的电路板无法直接向下放入外壳，因为静音开关会撞到后壁。Claude 算出，如果在安装时把电路板倾斜约 25 度就能装进去。它在 3D 模型中测试了这一点，并把该步骤加入了装配说明。

blocks.text: 在设计语音助手集线器的外壳时，Claude 计算出 25 毫米长的麦克风端口——让声音到达麦克风的开口——会在接近 3.4 kHz 处产生共振。它推断，这“正好落在语音频段内”，“虽不理想，但对语音助手用途仍可用。更好的方案是采用后部高、前部阶梯式降低的楔形外壳。”楔形设计把端口缩短到约 10 毫米，将共振频率提高到约 8.9 kHz，正好处于语音所用频段的边缘。Claude 还为扬声器电话编写了固件，让 LED 灯环随音频变响而变暗，以使设备保持在 Claude 为电路板设计的电流限制之内。

blocks.text: 面向真实制造的设计

inlines.text: 面向真实制造的设计

blocks.text: 在电子设计中，工程师必须在现实世界的约束下工作，也就是要确保工厂真的能造出他们想造的东西。为此他们会做两类检查：可制造性设计（DFM）检查，把电路板的几何形状与工厂的制造极限做比对；以及采购检查，确认分销商手头有这些元器件现货。

inlines.text: 在电子设计中，工程师必须在现实世界的约束下工作，也就是要确保工厂真的能造出他们想造的东西。为此他们会做两类检查：可制造性设计（DFM）检查，把电路板的几何形状与工厂的制造极限做比对；以及采购检查，确认分销商手头有这些元器件现货。

blocks.text: Claude 自己跑了这些检查，并把结果分成两类：需要修复的问题，以及可以忽略的提示。在对语音助手中枢的检查中，它标出了六处阻焊层（电路板上的保护涂层）过薄、无法制造。Claude 通过加宽阻焊层开口修复了这些问题，且没有移动任何元件。检查还把一个两个地（电流的共用回流路径）之间的连接标为错误，因为自动检查器没有识别出这个连接是刻意为之。Claude 正确判断出这不会影响性能，于是忽略了该提示。

blocks.text: 局限与下一步

inlines.text: 局限与下一步

blocks.text: 这三款设备目前都还是原型机：没有经过电气验证、天线调校、热测试或认证，也不是为量产而设计的。由于 Claude 并未接入测试设备，也没有连到制造和组装电路板的机器上，Diode 的工程师只能亲手搭建并测试这些原型。即便如此，过去一年里 Claude 在元器件布局与走线决策上的推理能力已有明显提升，如今它能在极少人工指导下设计电子设备，并帮助人们做出原型。其他模型也在这一方向上取得进展：OpenAI 最近发文介绍了如何用自家模型设计一款手持设备。这类工作有望帮助工程师更快地构建和测试新的硬件设计。

blocks.text: A little over a year ago, we began testing how well Claude could design basic electronic circuits. We collaborated with Diode Computers,1 a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, to train Claude on simple tasks—for example, on reading a chip’s datasheet and working out which parts a chip needs in order to run. The models we experimented with back then couldn’t reliably lay out a circuit board; they also struggled to design components that fit together. Now, Claude can both design and prototype electronic hardware from start to finish.

blocks.text: Engineering an electronic device requires working through many complex steps and practical constraints. You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build.

You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build.

blocks.text: To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry.

inlines.text: To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry.

blocks.text: For each design, we began by giving Claude a simple prompt that outlined what kind of device to build and its main hardware requirements. The prompt for the speakerphone, for example, asked for “a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna.” Claude proceeded to write the device’s specifications, draw clean visual schematics, choose where to place the components on a printed circuit board (PCB), route the copper connections between them, design a 3D-printable enclosure, code the firmware, and prepare a parts list. Diode assembled the circuit boards and ran the firmware, under Claude’s direction. The final result was a prototype of a speakerphone that still works after weeks of use.

Because the devices are early prototypes, we don’t yet know how they’ll hold up with continued use or whether they would pass commercial certifications.

blocks.text: Reasoning through geometric problems

inlines.text: Reasoning through geometric problems

blocks.text: The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them.

inlines.text: The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them.

blocks.text: Earlier models had struggled to decide how to arrange basic components—placing supporting parts too far from the chips they served, for example, or orienting connectors incorrectly. Fable 5.2, by contrast, produced more compact, practical layouts. It routed the most important connections first: those that carry high-speed signals or high currents, or that are sensitive to noise. For example, for the voice-assistant hub, Claude started by routing the USB and Ethernet connections, which transmit signals along pairs of tracks—thin strips of copper on the board. It routed one pair of tracks at a time, keeping the two tracks in each pair the same length and correctly spaced. It also added tuning patterns—small zigzags that lengthen a track so that signals arrive at the same time—and arranged the parts of the power supply to make it more efficient.

blocks.text: To demonstrate how much better Fable 5.2 is than earlier models at laying out circuit boards, we asked Diode to run PCB Gym—an internal benchmark that scores models based on how well they can place components and reroute connections on board designs whose layouts have been removed. Fable 5.2 scored 69% on the benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5 (Figure 2). It also performed better on BenchCAD 2.1, a public benchmark that tests whether models can rebuild 3D parts, assemblies, and circuit boards from engineering drawings and rendered images. Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, nearly double the score of its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1.

blocks.text: Revising designs

inlines.text: Revising designs

blocks.text: Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable.

inlines.text: Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable.

blocks.text: When Claude noticed one of its designs wasn’t working, it would change course without being prompted to do so. For instance, when designing the speakerphone’s circuit board, which has four layers of copper, it reassigned signals to different pins on two of the chips. This allowed the tracks under the speakerphone’s touch-sensitive controls to stay on a single layer without crossing one another. Later, when the back of the board became too crowded, Claude swapped the signals on interchangeable pins and laid out a whole corner of the board again, rather than patching the problem with extra jumps between layers.

blocks.text: Using software and documentation

inlines.text: Using software and documentation

blocks.text: When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place.2

inlines.text: When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place.

blocks.text: To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance.

inlines.text: To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance.

blocks.text: Instead, Claude wrote its own router: an algorithm that divides the board into a grid and searches it to find a clear path for each track. Within about half an hour, Claude had a router that could lay each long track in roughly a second. When Claude spotted an audio clock track running too close to the Ethernet tracks, it adjusted the router to leave more room around sensitive tracks.

blocks.text: Keeping track of constraints and downstream effects

inlines.text: Keeping track of constraints and downstream effects

blocks.text: Decisions made in one part of a design have downstream effects, which Claude kept track of. While designing each device’s enclosure, it wrote code to check that a 3D model of the circuit board would fit inside the enclosure without any components colliding. For example, it found that the speakerphone’s board couldn’t be lowered straight into the enclosure, because the mute switch would hit the back wall. Claude worked out that the board would fit if it was tilted by about 25 degrees during installation. It tested this in its 3D model and added the step to the assembly instructions.

inlines.text: Decisions made in one part of a design have downstream effects, which Claude kept track of. While designing each device’s enclosure, it wrote code to check that a 3D model of the circuit board would fit inside the enclosure without any components colliding. Claude worked out that the board would fit if it was tilted by about 25 degrees during installation. It tested this in its 3D model and added the step to the assembly instructions.

blocks.text: When designing the enclosure for the voice-assistant hub, Claude calculated that a 25 mm-long microphone port—the opening that lets sound reach the microphone—would resonate near 3.4 kHz. That is “right in the voice band,” it reasoned, “which is not ideal though still usable for voice assistant purposes. A better approach is a wedge-shaped enclosure that’s tall at the rear and steps down low at the front.” The wedge shape shortened the ports to about 10 mm, which raised the resonant frequency to about 8.9 kHz, at the very edge of the range used for speech. Claude also wrote firmware for the speakerphone that dims its ring of LED lights as the audio becomes louder, to keep the device under the electrical current limit Claude had designed into the board.

blocks.text: Designing for real-world manufacturing

inlines.text: Designing for real-world manufacturing

blocks.text: In electronics design, engineers have to work within the constraints of the real world. That is, they have to make sure a factory can actually make the thing they want to build. They do this by running two kinds of checks: design-for-manufacturing (DFM) checks, which compare a circuit board’s geometry with the factory’s manufacturing limits, and sourcing checks, which confirm that their distributors have the parts in stock.

inlines.text: In electronics design, engineers have to work within the constraints of the real world. That is, they have to make sure a factory can actually make the thing they want to build. They do this by running two kinds of checks: design-for-manufacturing (DFM) checks, which compare a circuit board’s geometry with the factory’s manufacturing limits, and sourcing checks, which confirm that their distributors have the parts in stock.

blocks.text: Claude ran these checks itself and sorted the results into problems that needed fixing and flags it could ignore. Its checks for the voice-assistant hub flagged six slivers of solder mask (the protective coating on a circuit board) as too thin to manufacture. Claude fixed them by widening the openings in the solder mask, without moving any parts. The checks also flagged a connection between two grounds (shared return paths for electrical current) as an error, because the automated checker hadn’t recognized that the connection was deliberate. Claude correctly reasoned that it wouldn’t affect performance and ignored the flag.

blocks.text: Diode manufactured all three boards directly from Claude’s design files, without any back-and-forth over adjustments. Factories and engineers often have to work through multiple rounds of manufacturing changes, and the Diode team told us they were surprised that they didn’t have to do this with Claude.

blocks.alt: Speakerphone circuit board, layer 1 (front): parts and signal tracks.

blocks.text: The speakerphone’s four copper layers. The dashed circle marks the touch wheel, where copper electrodes sense the user’s finger. Moving a track from one layer to another requires drilling a hole in the board, and under the touch wheel, that hole would go through an electrode. To avoid this, Claude kept each signal track under the wheel on a single layer, and it chose the chips’ pin assignments so that those tracks wouldn’t need to cross one another. It also kept the area around the Bluetooth antenna (the zigzag at the top) clear of other copper and holes on every layer, so nearby metal wouldn’t weaken its signal.

blocks.text: Limitations and next steps

inlines.text: Limitations and next steps

blocks.text: All three of these devices are still prototypes: they haven’t been through electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification, and they weren’t designed for mass production. Since Claude wasn’t connected to test equipment or to the machines that make and assemble circuit boards, engineers at Diode had to physically build and test the prototypes. Even so, over the past year, Claude has improved substantially at reasoning through decisions about component placement and routing, and it can now design electronics with minimal human guidance and help people build the prototypes. Other models are making progress here, too: OpenAI recently wrote about using its models to design a handheld device. Work like this could help engineers build and test new hardware designs faster.
